questions.text: How a dissection forms and how it is classified

steps.q:
**Sort the risk factors for aortic dissection:**
a The most common predisposing factor
b The two connective tissue disorders
c The other vessel-wall and lifestyle factors in the risk
diagram
d The demographic factor
steps.a:
- **HYPERTENSION** - most common predisposing factor
- **Marfan** syndrome, **Ehlers-Danlos** syndrome
- **Atherosclerosis** (changes vessel-wall structure),
**hyperlipidaemia**, **gene mutation**, **infectious disease**,
**smoking**
- **Elderly men** - males, 5th to 7th decades
bank_lines: Marrow: Aortic dissection or rupture is the leading cause of death in Marfan syndrome; mitral valve prolapse is commoner but far less lethal.

explain.intro: Step 1 continues with what weakens the wall. Two kinds of factor combine: things that raise the stress on the media (hypertension above all) and things that make the media weaker (connective-tissue disease, age). The one real question asks what Marfan patients die of.
why: a

**Hypertension: the most common predisposing factor.** Present in about three quarters of patients. Years of high pressure raise wall tension (Laplace) and damage the medial vasa vasorum, so the media degenerates.
b

**Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.** Marfan (fibrillin-1) and vascular Ehlers-Danlos (type III collagen) build a structurally weak media; dissection or rupture of the aorta is the leading cause of death in Marfan syndrome. Mitral valve prolapse is commoner in Marfan but rarely fatal.
c

**Atherosclerosis (changes vessel-wall structure), hyperlipidaemia, gene mutation, infectious disease, smoking.** Atherosclerosis causes penetrating ulcers more than classic dissection; genetic aortopathies (Loeys-Dietz, familial thoracic aortic disease) and aortitis weaken the wall directly.
d
**Elderly men: males, 5th to 7th decades.** Age itself thins and fragments the elastic media (AD-03).
mimic: Marfan: dissection vs mitral valve prolapse
MVP is the commonest cardiac finding; aortic dissection or rupture is the commonest cause of death.
traps: “Mitral valve prolapse or heart failure is the commonest cause of death in Marfan”
MVP is commoner but far less lethal; aortic dissection or rupture kills most Marfan patients, which is why their aortic root is replaced early.
decode: Most common cause of death in Marfan syndrome [Marrow]
Rupture of aortic dissection.
Most common predisposing factor for dissection [pattern]
Hypertension.
explain.punch: Hypertension is the commonest cause because it loads the media for years; connective-tissue disorders make the media weak from birth, and in Marfan the aorta, not the mitral valve, is what kills.

steps.q:
**Trace how an aortic dissection forms:**
a The layer in which the tear starts
b The layer blood then tracks through, and what it
creates
c The exact level within that layer, and what runs there
d The name for the resulting aorta
e The consequence for the true lumen
steps.a:
- Tear in the **INTIMA**
- Blood dissects through the **MEDIA**, creating a **FALSE
LUMEN**
- **Outer one-third of the media** - where the **vasa vasorum**
run
- **Double-barrelled aorta** - a true lumen and a false lumen
- False lumen **compresses the true lumen** → impaired flow
→ **MALPERFUSION SYNDROME**

explain.intro: Step 2 begins with the tear itself. Once blood enters the wall, the false lumen it creates is what causes every later complication. Not asked directly, but each complication card builds on this sequence.
why: a
**Tear in the intima.** Usually in the right lateral wall of the ascending aorta a few centimetres above the valve, or just beyond the left subclavian, where the wall stress is highest.
b
**Blood dissects through the media, creating a false lumen.** Pulsatile flow drives a column of blood along the weak plane, antegrade and sometimes retrograde.
c

**Outer one-third of the media, where the vasa vasorum run.** The plane lies in the outer media, so the outer wall of the false lumen is thin; that is why the false lumen can rupture outward into the pericardium, pleura or mediastinum. A bleed from the vasa vasorum without an intimal tear is an intramural haematoma.
d
**Double-barrelled aorta: a true lumen and a false lumen.** The intimal flap that separates them is what CT and echo look for (AD-17).
e

**False lumen compresses the true lumen → impaired flow → malperfusion syndrome.** The false lumen often carries higher pressure, so it bulges into the true lumen (dynamic obstruction) or extends into a branch and occludes it (static obstruction) (AD-05).
mimic: Classic dissection vs intramural haematoma
Dissection has an intimal tear and a flap with flow in two lumens; IMH is crescentic wall thickening with no flap and no flow.
traps: “The false lumen lies between intima and media”
The plane is within the media, in its outer third.
decode: Layer in which the cleavage plane forms [pattern]
The media (outer third).
explain.punch: An intimal tear lets blood split the outer media; the false lumen then either ruptures outward through its thin wall or squeezes the true lumen and its branches, and that is the whole disease.

steps.q:
**For propagation of a dissection, explain:**
a The force that drives it, and how it is expressed
b Which haemodynamic variable influences it more
c The therapeutic consequence
steps.a:
- **SHEAR STRESS** - a function of pressure over time, **dP/dt**
- Influenced more by **HEART RATE** than by mean arterial
pressure
- **Lowering the heart rate is critical** to reduce propagation

explain.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Propagation and dP/dt
explain.intro: Step 2 asks what makes the tear spread. The answer, the steepness of each pressure upstroke, is why the drug order in AD-19 matters. The one real question is a type A dissection with a heart rate of 112, and a third of the cohort chose something other than a beta-blocker.
why: a

**Shear stress, a function of pressure over time, dP/dt.** Each systole drives a pressure wave into the flap; the faster pressure rises, the harder the column of blood pushes into the plane of the dissection and the further it travels. Mean pressure alone does not capture this.
b

**Influenced more by heart rate than by mean arterial pressure.** A faster heart means more upstrokes per minute and a steeper upstroke (more contractility, shorter ejection time). Halving the rate halves the number of pushes into the tear.
c

**Lowering the heart rate is critical to reduce propagation.** Hence a beta-blocker first, to HR about 60, before any vasodilator. A vasodilator alone lowers pressure but triggers baroreflex tachycardia and a stronger contraction, which raises dP/dt.
mimic: Dissection vs other hypertensive emergencies

In most hypertensive emergencies the target is the pressure; in dissection it is dP/dt, so the heart rate is controlled first and the pressure is lowered much further and faster (SBP <120 within the first hour).
traps: “Start nitroprusside: the BP of 182/93 is the problem” (38% of the cohort chose something other than esmolol)
Nitroprusside alone causes reflex tachycardia and raises dP/dt; it is added only after the beta-blocker.
“Get a TEE or consult cardiology first”
CT has already made the diagnosis; more imaging or a consult only delays anti-impulse therapy and surgery.
decode: Type A on CT, HR 112, BP 182/93, AR murmur — next best step? [DocT GT]
Start an esmolol infusion (62%), then arrange surgery.
Which variable most influences propagation? [pattern]
Heart rate (dP/dt), more than MAP.
explain.punch: A dissection spreads with every steep upstroke, so the heart rate is lowered first; a vasodilator given alone makes the heart beat faster and harder, and the tear spreads.

steps.q:
**For the true and false lumens, give:**
a The usual position of the true lumen
b The branches that usually arise from the true lumen
c The branch that often arises from the false lumen
steps.a:
- True lumen is **ANTEROMEDIAL**
- **Coeliac**, **superior mesenteric** and **RIGHT renal** arteries
- **LEFT renal artery** - often from the false lumen
bank_lines: DocT GT: On echo the TRUE lumen expands in systole with systolic forward colour flow in phase with the cardiac cycle; the FALSE lumen is usually larger, compressed in systole, with slow, delayed or reversed flow, spontaneous contrast or thrombus, and 'cobwebs' (residual media strands).

explain.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → True vs false lumen
explain.intro: Step 2: telling the lumens apart matters because TEVAR has to land in the true lumen and because the branches arising from the false lumen are the ones at risk. The real question asks how echo separates them; nearly half of the cohort picked a feature of the false lumen.
why: a

**True lumen is anteromedial.** In the descending aorta the false lumen usually spirals along the outer (left posterolateral) curve. Position helps on CT but is not reliable; flow and behaviour through the cardiac cycle are better.
b
**Coeliac, superior mesenteric and right renal arteries.** These usually stay with the true lumen.
c
**Left renal artery, often from the false lumen.** That is why left kidney malperfusion and AKI are common in type B and DeBakey I dissections.
mimic: Which lumen is larger?
The false lumen usually is; a small lumen is not proof it is false.
traps: “The false lumen is usually smaller” or “expands in systole” (56% right)
Both describe the true lumen in reverse: the false lumen is usually larger and is compressed in systole.
“Cobwebs are seen in the true lumen”
Cobwebs (strands of residual media) are a feature of the false lumen.
decode: Descending dissection — most helpful echo feature for the true lumen? [DocT GT]
Colour Doppler flow in phase with the cardiac cycle, systolic expansion (56%).
Which renal artery usually arises from the false lumen? [pattern]
Left.
explain.punch: The true lumen expands and fills forward in systole; the false lumen is larger, slower, has cobwebs, and often feeds the left renal artery.

table.title: Echo: true vs false lumen
head: Feature
True lumen
False lumen
rows: Systolic, forward, in phase with the cardiac cycle
Slow, delayed or reversed; spontaneous contrast or thrombus

steps.q:
**Give the extent of each DeBakey type:**
a Type I
b Type II
c Type III
steps.a:
- **Type I** - ascending **AND** descending aorta
- **Type II** - ascending aorta **ONLY**
- **Type III** - descending aorta **ONLY**
**DeBakey I**
**DeBakey II**
**DeBakey III**
Coloured = dissected. Third arch branch = left subclavian.
**Stanford A**
**Stanford B**
bank_lines: DocT GT: DeBakey type III is subdivided: IIIa is confined to the descending THORACIC aorta (above the diaphragm), IIIb extends below the diaphragm into the abdominal aorta; both are Stanford B.

explain.intro: Step 3: DeBakey classifies by where the dissection starts and how far it extends. Both real questions were answered badly (12% and 38%), because each needs you to work out which branches and complications are anatomically possible.
why: a

**Type I: ascending AND descending aorta.** Starts in the ascending aorta and runs at least to the arch, usually beyond. Every complication is possible: coronary, cerebral, AR, tamponade, visceral, renal, spinal and limb.
b
**Type II: ascending aorta ONLY.** Confined proximal to the innominate artery. It can cause AR, tamponade and coronary occlusion, but it cannot reach the mesenteric or renal arteries.
c

**Type III: descending aorta ONLY.** Starts beyond the left subclavian. IIIa stops above the diaphragm (descending thoracic only); IIIb extends below it into the abdominal aorta. Both are Stanford B. It cannot cause AR, tamponade or coronary occlusion (unless it extends backwards into the arch).
mimic: DeBakey IIIa vs IIIb
IIIa is limited to the thoracic descending aorta; IIIb extends below the diaphragm.
DeBakey II vs Stanford A
All DeBakey II is Stanford A, but Stanford A also includes DeBakey I.
traps: “A dissection of the descending thoracic aorta is DeBakey III” (bare III, or IIIb; 38% right)
With the subdivision offered, thoracic-only is IIIa; IIIb goes below the diaphragm.
“Which pairing is NOT correct?” — only one option looks wrong (12% right)

Two are wrong: DeBakey II (ascending only) cannot cause high lactate, high INR and AKI from visceral malperfusion, and DeBakey III (descending only) cannot cause a new AR murmur. DocT keys A (the DeBakey II pairing); pick A.
decode: Dissection of the descending thoracic aorta — DeBakey type? [DocT GT]
IIIa (38%).
Which complication–classification pairing is wrong? [DocT GT]
Visceral malperfusion with DeBakey II (12%); AR with DeBakey III is also wrong.
explain.punch: DeBakey I is everywhere, II is ascending only, III is descending only (IIIa thoracic, IIIb below the diaphragm), and each type can cause only the complications its segment supplies.

steps.q:
**For the Stanford classification, give:**
a The definition of type A
b The definition of type B
c How the DeBakey types map onto Stanford
d The single feature that decides the Stanford type
steps.a:
- **Type A** - involves the aorta **proximal to the left
subclavian** origin
- **Type B** - involves the aorta **distal to the left subclavian**
origin
**DeBakey** | **Stanford**
**I (ascending + descending)** | **A**
**II (ascending only)** | **A**
**III (descending only)** | **B**
- Deciding feature: is the **ASCENDING** aorta involved?

explain.intro: Step 3: Stanford simplifies DeBakey to the one question that decides treatment: is the ascending aorta involved? The one real question is the GT pairing question shared with AD-09.
why: a

**Type A: involves the aorta proximal to the left subclavian origin.** Strictly, type A is any involvement of the ascending aorta, wherever the tear starts; an arch-only dissection is non-A non-B (AD-11).
b
**Type B: involves the aorta distal to the left subclavian origin.** Without ascending involvement.
c
**DeBakey I and II = Stanford A; DeBakey III = Stanford B.** DeBakey adds extent; Stanford keeps only what changes management.
d
**Deciding feature: is the ascending aorta involved?** If yes, the risks are tamponade, coronary occlusion and AR, which only surgery fixes, so type A is a surgical emergency (AD-12).
mimic: Stanford A from a descending tear
A tear in the descending aorta that extends backwards into the ascending aorta is still type A.
traps: “Elevated troponin cannot occur in Stanford A”
It can: the flap can occlude a coronary ostium. Troponin with Stanford A is a correct pairing.
decode: Pairing of complications with Stanford and DeBakey types [DocT GT]
Troponin rise with Stanford A and hemiplegia with DeBakey I are correct pairings.
explain.punch: Stanford asks only whether the ascending aorta is involved, because that is what decides between the operating theatre and the ICU.

steps.q:
**For the TEM classification adopted by the**
**2024 ESC guidelines, give:**
a What T, E and M stand for
b The three T categories
c The gap in Stanford it fills
steps.a:
- **T** = Type of dissection • **E** = Entry tear location • **M** =
Malperfusion (carries prognostic and therapeutic weight)
- **Type A • Type B • non-A non-B**
- Arch involvement WITHOUT ascending involvement -
unclassifiable in Stanford, now **non-A non-B**
Added card: not in the notes. Source: 2024 ESC Guidelines on
peripheral arterial and aortic diseases.

explain.intro: Step 3 ends with the classification the 2024 ESC guideline adopted. It keeps Stanford’s logic but adds where the entry tear is and whether organs are ischaemic, because both change the operation. Not asked yet.
why: a

**T = Type of dissection; E = Entry tear location; M = Malperfusion (carries prognostic and therapeutic weight).** E0 means no entry seen; E1 entry in the ascending aorta (zone 0), E2 in the arch, E3 in the descending aorta. M0 none, M1 coronary, M2 supra-aortic, M3 spinal, visceral, renal or limb, each marked + if clinically symptomatic.
b
**Type A, Type B, non-A non-B.** ESC 2024 defines non-A non-B as dissections limited to the arch, or retrograde from the descending aorta into the arch, without involving the ascending aorta.
c

**Arch involvement WITHOUT ascending involvement: unclassifiable in Stanford, now non-A non-B.** These behave between A and B: they rarely need emergency sternotomy but often need arch or hybrid repair.
mimic: Non-A non-B vs type B
Type B stays distal to the left subclavian; non-A non-B involves the arch without the ascending aorta.
traps: “TEM replaced the need to assess malperfusion clinically”
M is graded with a + sign for clinical signs, so the bedside picture is part of the class.
decode: Classification used by ESC 2024 with a non-A non-B category [pattern]
TEM (type, entry, malperfusion).
explain.punch: TEM keeps Stanford’s A and B, adds non-A non-B for arch-only dissection, and records the entry tear and malperfusion because they decide the operation.

questions.text: Recognising it, and the ACS trap

steps.q:
**For the clinical picture of aortic dissection,**
**give:**
a The pain
b The usual blood pressure
c The inter-arm BP difference that is significant
d The murmur and its cause
e The signs of tamponade
f Hypotension - early or late sign?
steps.a:
- Sudden-onset severe **"ripping" / "tearing"** chest pain,
back pain radiating to the chest
- **HIGH** blood pressure
- Difference between arms **>20 mmHg** (also radial pulse
deficit)
- **Diastolic murmur** - aortic insufficiency
- **Low BP, muffled heart sounds**
- **LATE** sign (also collapse / syncope; focal neuro deficit →
limb weakness, paraesthesia)

explain.intro: Step 4 is recognition at the bedside. The signs follow the anatomy: pain from the tearing wall, pressure differences from compressed branches, a diastolic murmur from a disrupted valve, and shock from tamponade or rupture. The linked real question shows a classic picture and asks for the imaging test, where DocT’s key is outdated (AD-17).
why: a

**Sudden-onset severe ‘ripping’ or ‘tearing’ chest pain, back pain radiating to the chest.** The key feature is that the pain is maximal at onset (85% abrupt in IRAD); only about half call it tearing, and sharp is the commonest word. Anterior chest pain suggests type A, back or abdominal pain type B; about 6% have no pain.
b
**HIGH blood pressure.** Typical of type B; type A patients are more often normotensive or hypotensive because of tamponade, AR or rupture.
c

**Difference between arms >20 mmHg (also radial pulse deficit).** The flap compresses the subclavian or innominate; a pulse deficit is seen in only about 15%, so its absence does not exclude dissection. Measure the pressure in both arms before giving thrombolysis.
d

**Diastolic murmur: aortic insufficiency.** Heard in about a third. The flap dilates the root, tears the commissures or prolapses through the valve. A murmur at the right sternal border points to root dilatation, as in the vignette.
e
**Low BP, muffled heart sounds.** Rupture into the pericardium; with raised JVP this is Beck’s triad.
f

**LATE sign (also collapse or syncope; focal neuro deficit → limb weakness, paraesthesia).** Hypotension means tamponade, rupture, severe AR or coronary occlusion, and it carries the worst prognosis. Syncope (about 9%) often means tamponade or carotid involvement.
mimic: Dissection vs ACS pain
Dissection: maximal at onset, tearing or sharp, moving to the back, pulse or pressure asymmetry. ACS: builds over minutes, pressing, with no asymmetry.
traps: “TEE is the preferred test” for a stable patient with BP 205/110 (DocT key; 40% chose it)
The key is outdated: ESC 2024 makes ECG-gated CT neck to pelvis first line (I, C). For a stable patient choose CT; TEE is for the unstable or for the theatre.
“No pulse deficit, so no dissection”
Pulse deficits are present in only about 15%.
decode: Tearing pain to the jaw, BP 205/110, diastolic murmur, widened mediastinum — preferred test? [DocT QBank]
CT angiography (DocT keys TEE, 40%).
Hypotension in dissection: early or late? [pattern]
Late, and ominous (tamponade, rupture, AR).
explain.punch: Pain maximal at onset with a pressure difference or a new diastolic murmur means dissection; high BP is usual, and hypotension means the aorta has ruptured into the pericardium or the valve has failed.

steps.q:
**For the overlap between aortic dissection**
**and ACS, give:**
a The most common misdiagnosis
b The ECG changes dissection can produce, and when
c Why troponin may rise
d Why the misdiagnosis is catastrophic
steps.a:
- Misdiagnosed as **ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME** -
consider dissection once ACS is ruled out
- Non-specific **ST-T changes** and **T-wave inversion**,
especially when the dissection involves the **coronary
artery origins**
- Coronary origin involvement → true myocardial injury,
mimicking MI
- **THROMBOLYSIS** given for a presumed MI can be
catastrophic

explain.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Dissection mimicking ACS
explain.intro: Step 4: the commonest misdiagnosis, and the one with the worst consequence, because the treatment for ACS can kill a dissection patient. Not asked directly here, but the GT question on AD-17 is built on this overlap.
why: a
**Misdiagnosed as ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME; consider dissection once ACS is ruled out.** Both happen in older hypertensive men with severe chest pain, and most dissection ECGs are abnormal.
b

**Non-specific ST-T changes and T-wave inversion, especially when the dissection involves the coronary artery origins.** In IRAD, 41% had non-specific ST-T changes and 15% ischaemic changes, but only about 3% a new infarct pattern. When it happens, it is usually the right coronary ostium, so an inferior STEMI.
c
**Coronary origin involvement → true myocardial injury, mimicking MI.** Troponin also rises from hypotension, tachycardia and LVH strain, so a positive troponin does not exclude dissection.
d

**THROMBOLYSIS given for a presumed MI can be catastrophic.** Lysis or heparin turns the false lumen into a bleeding cavity and can cause tamponade. Aortic dissection is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis (MI-53), and the pressure in both arms is checked before lysis.
mimic: Inferior STEMI from RCA occlusion vs from type A dissection
Look for a pressure or pulse difference, AR murmur, widened mediastinum or effusion on bedside echo; image the aorta before lysis or the catheter lab.
traps: “Normal troponin excludes dissection” or “raised troponin confirms ACS”
Troponin is often normal in dissection and can be raised by it; it does not separate the two.
decode: Inferior STEMI with BP difference between arms — next step? [pattern]
Image the aorta (CT) before thrombolysis or anticoagulation.
explain.punch: Dissection imitates ACS, usually through the right coronary, and the treatment for ACS can kill it, so check both arms and look at the aorta before lysis.

steps.q:
**Map each arterial bed to its malperfusion**
**presentation.**
a Coronary
b Cerebral
c Spinal cord
d Renal
e Visceral (mesenteric)
f Limb
steps.a:
**Bed** | **Presentation**
**Coronary** | MI or acute coronary syndrome
**Cerebral** | Stroke / stroke-like symptoms
**Spinal cord** | Paraplegia or paraparesis
**Renal** | Oliguria and acute kidney injury
**Visceral** | Gut ischaemia - abdominal pain, lactic acidosis
**Limb** | Numbness, weakness or pain

explain.intro: Step 2: when the false lumen compresses or extends into a branch, the organ supplied by that branch fails, and the presentation follows the branch. Not asked directly, but malperfusion turns a dissection into a ‘complicated’ one (AD-13) and drives the GT pairing question on AD-09.
why: a
**Coronary: MI or acute coronary syndrome.** When a coronary is involved it is usually the right ostium, giving an inferior ST-elevation pattern (AD-15). Only type A can do this.
b
**Cerebral: stroke or stroke-like symptoms.** Extension into the innominate or left carotid; again a type A (or arch) feature.
c
**Spinal cord: paraplegia or paraparesis.** Intercostal arteries arising from the false lumen lose flow; the artery of Adamkiewicz (T8–T12) is the critical one (AD-28).
d
**Renal: oliguria and acute kidney injury.** The left renal artery often arises from the false lumen (AD-07).
e
**Visceral: gut ischaemia, with abdominal pain and lactic acidosis.** Coeliac or superior mesenteric involvement; ESC 2024 gives mesenteric malperfusion a mortality of 65–95%.
f
**Limb: numbness, weakness or pain.** Iliac or subclavian compression gives a pulse deficit and an inter-arm or arm-leg pressure difference.
mimic: Coronary or cerebral vs visceral or renal malperfusion
Coronary and cerebral need the ascending aorta or arch (type A); visceral, renal and leg need the descending or abdominal aorta (DeBakey I or III).
traps: “Mesenteric malperfusion causes early abdominal tenderness”
Pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen with rising lactate is the early picture; peritonism is late.
decode: New paraplegia in a descending dissection — which artery? [pattern]
Artery of Adamkiewicz (intercostals T8–T12).
Dissection with rising lactate and abdominal pain [pattern]
Mesenteric malperfusion: the coeliac or SMA is compromised.
explain.punch: Each branch the false lumen squeezes gives its own syndrome, and which syndromes are possible depends on which part of the aorta is dissected.

steps.q:
**For bedside tests in aortic dissection, give:**
a The chest X-ray finding and how often it is seen
b The danger of a normal chest X-ray
c The full blood count changes, and why
d When lactate rises
steps.a:
- **Widened mediastinum - 50%**
- Falsely reassuring → **missed diagnosis**
- **Leukocytosis** or **thrombocytopenia** (platelet
consumption)
- **Gut ischaemia** - compromised **coeliac or superior
mesenteric** arteries
bank_lines: Marrow: Other chest X-ray signs of dissection: double or irregular aortic contour and inward displacement of intimal calcification >5 mm from the outer aortic wall (calcium sign).

explain.intro: Step 4: the bedside tests raise or lower suspicion but never settle it. The one real question asks which chest X-ray sign is seen.
why: a

**Widened mediastinum: 50%.** IRAD found a widened mediastinum in about 62% and an abnormal aortic contour in about 50%. Other signs: a double or irregular aortic contour, displacement of intimal calcification more than 5 mm inside the outer aortic wall (calcium sign; some texts use 1 cm), and a left pleural effusion.
b
**Falsely reassuring → missed diagnosis.** About 12% of chest X-rays are completely normal (IRAD). ESC 2024: an X-ray and ECG are done to exclude other causes, and normal findings must not delay CT.
c

**Leukocytosis or thrombocytopenia (platelet consumption).** The false lumen is a large thrombogenic surface; platelets and fibrinogen are consumed and D-dimer rises. A D-dimer under 500 ng/mL makes acute dissection unlikely (ESC 2024).
d
**Gut ischaemia: compromised coeliac or superior mesenteric arteries.** Lactate rises with mesenteric malperfusion, or with shock; a rising lactate after repair calls for repeat CT (AD-26).
mimic: Widened mediastinum: dissection vs traumatic aortic injury
Trauma: deceleration injury at the isthmus; dissection: spontaneous pain in a hypertensive patient. Both go to CT.
traps: “A normal chest X-ray excludes dissection”
About one in eight are normal.
decode: Feature of dissection on chest X-ray [Marrow]
Abnormal aortic contour (also a widened mediastinum, calcium sign).
Low-risk patient with D-dimer <500 ng/mL [pattern]
Dissection unlikely.
explain.punch: The X-ray shows a widened mediastinum or abnormal contour in about half to two thirds, is normal in one in eight, and can never rule dissection out; only CT does that.

steps.q:
**For each imaging test in suspected**
**dissection, give its role and limitation:**
a Transthoracic echo
b Transoesophageal echo
c CT aortogram
d MR angiography
steps.a:
**Test** | **Role / limitation**
**TTE** | Shows **severe AR** if root or valve involved; **may miss** the dissection
**TEE** | **Superior to TTE** - sees nearly all the aorta (blind spot: distal ascending aorta and proximal arch, behind the trachea); useful if CT contraindicated or patient cannot be transported
**CT aortogram** | The **DEFINITIVE** test - whole aorta; preferred over routine contrast CT chest or CT pulmonary angiography
**MR angiography** | Detailed, but **slow** - unsuitable for unstable patients
2024 ESC: first-line imaging is ECG-gated contrast CT from
neck to pelvis (I, C); TEE to guide perioperative management (I,
C).
bank_lines: Marrow: TEE signs of dissection: an undulating intimal flap separating true and false lumens, colour-flow in both lumens, entry/exit tears, false-lumen stasis or thrombus, and intramural haematoma (crescentic wall thickening without a flap).

explain.intro: Step 4 ends with the test that decides. Four real questions ask which test to choose and what it shows, and the choice depends on one thing: whether the patient can safely go to the scanner. DocT’s QBank key is outdated, and its GT question shows how an effusion leads people into a lethal step.
why: a

**TTE: shows severe AR if the root or valve is involved; may miss the dissection.** It sees the root, valve, pericardium and LV well but only parts of the aorta. Its role is the first bedside look: an effusion, AR or a dilated root in a patient with chest pain means type A until proved otherwise.
b

**TEE: superior to TTE, sees nearly all the aorta (blind spot: distal ascending aorta and proximal arch, behind the trachea); useful if CT is contraindicated or the patient cannot be transported.** It shows an undulating flap separating the lumens, colour flow in both lumens, entry and exit tears, false-lumen stasis or thrombus, and intramural haematoma (crescentic wall thickening without a flap). ESC 2024 recommends it to guide peri-operative management (I, C): in theatre it confirms the entry tear, valve mechanism and coronary involvement.
c

**CT aortogram: the DEFINITIVE test, whole aorta; preferred over routine contrast CT chest or CT pulmonary angiography.** ESC 2024 first-line test: ECG-gated contrast CT from neck to pelvis (I, C), sensitivity 100% and specificity 98%. ECG gating removes motion artefact at the root that can mimic a flap; neck to pelvis shows the extent, the branches and malperfusion.
d
**MR angiography: detailed but slow, unsuitable for unstable patients.** It is used for follow-up and when contrast or radiation must be avoided.
mimic: Stable vs unstable suspected dissection
Stable → CT; too unstable to move → TEE in the ED or theatre (with bedside TTE first). The same split applies to PE: stable → CTPA, unstable → bedside echo.
CT aortogram vs CTPA
A CTPA times contrast for the pulmonary arteries and can miss the aorta; a suspected dissection needs an aortic (ECG-gated) protocol.
traps: “TEE is the preferred investigation” for a stable patient with BP 205/110 (DocT key; 40% chose it)
The key is outdated. ESC 2024 makes CT first line; TEE is for the unstable, CT contraindication, or in theatre. If the patient is stable and CT is offered, pick CT.
“Pericardiocentesis” or “coronary angiography” for chest pain, BP 200/89, negative troponin and an effusion (24% right)

The effusion with a normal troponin and hypertension points to type A dissection; pericardiocentesis can restore pressure and speed rupture, and coronary angiography delays surgery. Image the aorta with CT, then go to theatre.
“TEE sees the whole aorta”
The trachea hides the distal ascending aorta and proximal arch.
decode: Stable, tearing pain, BP 205/110, AR murmur, wide mediastinum — preferred test? [DocT QBank]
CT angiography (DocT keys TEE; 40%).
Chest pain, BP 200/89, troponin negative, moderate effusion on POCUS — next step? [DocT GT]
Contrast CT of the chest (24%), not pericardiocentesis.
CT angiogram with an intimal flap and two lumens [DocT QBank]
Aortic dissection (68%).
TEE findings of dissection [Marrow]
All: flap, flow in both lumens, entry and exit tears, false-lumen thrombus, IMH.
explain.punch: If the patient can go to the scanner, ECG-gated CT from neck to pelvis is the test; TEE is for the patient who cannot be moved and for the theatre; and an effusion with chest pain and hypertension is dissection until CT says otherwise.

questions.text: Treating it: the drug sequence, surgery or stent

steps.q:
**For initial stabilisation of acute aortic**
**dissection, give:**
a The analgesic of choice and why
b The heart rate target
c The systolic BP target
d The lines needed for monitoring, and why
steps.a:
- **Opioid (morphine)** - cuts sympathetic drive → prevents
tachycardia and further shear stress (dP/dt)
- HR **<60 bpm**
- SBP **<120 mmHg**
- **Arterial and central lines** - avoid rapid BP fluctuations

explain.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Stabilisation and targets
explain.intro: Step 5 begins anti-impulse therapy: pain, heart rate and pressure, in that order, because each drives dP/dt. The one real question tests the drug sequence, which is covered in AD-19.
why: a

**Opioid (morphine): cuts sympathetic drive → prevents tachycardia and further shear stress (dP/dt).** Pain releases catecholamines that raise heart rate and contractility; analgesia is part of reaching the targets (ESC 2024: adequate pain control, I, C). Persistent pain despite analgesia means the dissection is still extending (AD-13).
b
**HR <60 bpm.** ESC 2024: HR ≤60 b.p.m. (I, B). The 2022 ACC/AHA guideline gives 60–80 b.p.m. (class 1, C-LD). In the exam, ‘about 60’ fits both.
c

**SBP <120 mmHg.** Both guidelines; ACC/AHA adds ‘or the lowest BP that maintains end-organ perfusion’ (class 1, C-LD), and most protocols aim to reach it within about the first hour. ESC 2024 accepts a higher pressure when an organ is malperfused. Heart rate first, then pressure.
d

**Arterial and central lines: avoid rapid BP fluctuations.** An arterial line, ideally in the arm with the higher pressure (the other arm may be reading a compressed subclavian), allows titration of short-acting infusions beat to beat; a central line is for vasoactive drugs.
mimic: ESC vs ACC/AHA heart-rate target
ESC 2024: ≤60; ACC/AHA 2022: 60–80. Same SBP target, below 120.
traps: “Labetalol alone is wrong because it is not esmolol”
Labetalol is an acceptable first-line agent (it blocks β and α1); the key prefers esmolol then nicardipine because it follows the beta-blocker-before-vasodilator rule.
“Put the arterial line in the arm with the lower pressure”
Use the arm with the higher reading; the lower one may reflect a compressed branch and underestimate the true pressure.
decode: Type B, BP 210/115, HR 102 — initial drugs? [DocT GT]
Esmolol followed by nicardipine (59%).
HR and SBP targets in acute dissection [pattern]
HR about 60 (ESC ≤60; ACC/AHA 60–80), SBP <120 mmHg.
explain.punch: Treat the pain, slow the heart to about 60, then bring the systolic below 120, watching an arterial line in the arm with the higher pressure.

steps.q:
**Route the drug choice in acute dissection:**
a The first-line class and its three agents
b The alternatives if beta-blockers are contraindicated
c The agents for refractory hypertension
d The rule for using those agents, and why
e Why NTG / SNP are avoided as first line
steps.a:
- **IV BETA-BLOCKERS**: **labetalol** (α1 + β1 + β2), **esmolol**
(short-acting β1, infusion), **metoprolol** (small boluses)
- **Non-dihydropyridine CCB** (diltiazem); ACE inhibitor also
considered
- **Nitroglycerin** or **sodium nitroprusside**
- ONLY **after / with a beta-blocker** - to block reflex
tachycardia
- Reflex tachycardia ↑ dP/dt → **propagation**

explain.intro: Step 5’s core: five real questions all test one rule, beta-blocker before vasodilator. Each distractor is a drug that lowers pressure without slowing the heart, or a slow route of giving the right drug.
why: a

**IV BETA-BLOCKERS: labetalol (α1 + β1 + β2), esmolol (short-acting β1, infusion), metoprolol (small boluses).** Beta-blockade lowers heart rate and contractility, so dP/dt falls before pressure does. Esmolol is preferred when the patient may not tolerate beta-blockade (asthma, borderline pressure, AR) because it wears off in about 10–20 minutes. Labetalol alone can reach both targets, since it also vasodilates; ESC 2024 calls IV labetalol the usual first choice, with esmolol an option.
b

**Non-dihydropyridine CCB (diltiazem); ACE inhibitor also considered.** ESC 2024 (IIa, B) and ACC/AHA 2022 (2a, B-NR): an IV non-DHP calcium blocker for rate control if beta-blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated. Diltiazem and verapamil slow the sinus and AV nodes; dihydropyridines do not.
c
**Nitroglycerin or sodium nitroprusside.** Nicardipine (a dihydropyridine) is the other common choice and the one used in the DocT keys.
d
**ONLY after or with a beta-blocker, to block reflex tachycardia.** Once the rate is controlled, the vasodilator takes the systolic below 120.
e

**Reflex tachycardia ↑ dP/dt → propagation.** Vasodilation drops the pressure, the baroreflex speeds the heart and strengthens contraction, and the shear on the flap rises even though the cuff reading has fallen.
mimic: Diltiazem vs nicardipine
Diltiazem (non-DHP) slows the heart and replaces a beta-blocker; nicardipine (DHP) only vasodilates and must follow one.
traps: “IV nitroprusside alone” or “nicardipine infusion alone” (76–83% right)
Monotherapy with a vasodilator causes reflex tachycardia; it is used only after a beta-blocker.
“Oral metoprolol”
Right class, wrong route: the targets must be reached within the hour, so IV.
“Sublingual nitroglycerin then an ACE inhibitor”
Uncontrolled, with no rate control; neither is first line.
“Labetalol alone is wrong” (GT4/GT5; 59–83% right)
Labetalol alone is acceptable; DocT keys esmolol then nicardipine, so pick that when both are offered.
decode: First-line drug to limit propagation [DocT GT]
IV esmolol (76%).
Type A, BP 180/100 — first-line agent? [DocT GT]
Esmolol infusion (73%).
Type B, BP 210/115, HR 102 — initial pharmacological management? [DocT GT ×2]
Esmolol followed by nicardipine (59%, 83%).
Dissection with arm BP difference on CTA — next step? [Marrow]
Esmolol.
explain.punch: Every dissection drug question has the same answer: an IV beta-blocker first (or diltiazem if one cannot be given), and a vasodilator only once the heart rate is controlled.

steps.q:
**Give the IV doses of the first-line**
**beta-blockers:**
a Esmolol
b Labetalol - bolus
c Labetalol - infusion
d Metoprolol
steps.a:
**Drug** | **IV dose**
**Esmolol (β1)** | Bolus **500 mcg/kg over 1 min**, then **50 mcg/kg/min**, titrate up to **300 mcg/kg/min**
**Labetalol bolus** | **20 mg over 2 min**, then **20-80 mg every 10 min**
**Labetalol infusion** | Load **20 mg**, then **1-2 mg/min**
**Metoprolol** | **5 mg over 2 min**, repeat every 5 min, up to **3 doses**

explain.intro: Step 5: the doses of the drugs that come first. The one real question asks only which drug to start, but the doses show why esmolol is the safest titratable choice.
why: a

**Esmolol (β1): bolus 500 mcg/kg over 1 min, then 50 mcg/kg/min, titrated up to 300 mcg/kg/min.** Red-cell esterases clear it with a half-life of about 9 minutes, so its effect stops within about 20 minutes, which makes it the safest choice if AR, asthma or low pressure might make beta-blockade risky.
b

**Labetalol bolus: 20 mg over 2 min, then 20–80 mg every 10 min.** The label gives repeat doses of 40–80 mg every 10 minutes, to a cumulative maximum of 300 mg. Its β:α ratio is about 7:1 IV, so it slows the heart and dilates the arteries.
c
**Labetalol infusion: load 20 mg, then 1–2 mg/min.** Its half-life is 5–8 hours, so it is harder to reverse than esmolol.
d
**Metoprolol: 5 mg over 2 min, repeated every 5 min, up to 3 doses.** Bolus-only control is less smooth, which is why it ranks behind the infusions.
mimic: Esmolol vs labetalol
Esmolol: pure β1, minutes-long, infusion; labetalol: β plus α1, hours-long, boluses or infusion.
traps: “Oral metoprolol to limit propagation”
Too slow; the IV route is needed to reach targets within the hour.
decode: First-line IV agent to limit propagation [DocT GT]
IV esmolol (76%).
Esmolol loading dose [pattern]
500 mcg/kg over 1 minute, then 50 mcg/kg/min.
explain.punch: Esmolol is the easiest beta-blocker to titrate because a 500 mcg/kg load and a 50–300 mcg/kg/min infusion wear off within minutes; labetalol (ESC 2024’s usual first choice) and IV metoprolol work equally well but last much longer.

steps.q:
**Give the IV doses of the second-line agents**
**and vasodilators:**
a Diltiazem
b Nicardipine
c Sodium nitroprusside
d Nitroglycerin
steps.a:
**Drug** | **IV dose**
**Diltiazem (non-DHP)** | **0.25 mg/kg over 2 min**, then **5-10 mg/h**, up to **15 mg/h**
**Nicardipine (DHP)** | **5 mg/h**, increase **2.5 mg/h every 5-15 min**, max **15 mg/h**
**Nitroprusside** | **0.3 mcg/kg/min**, max **10 mcg/kg/min** (no more than 10 min at max) - **cyanide toxicity**, unsuitable for prolonged use
**Nitroglycerin** | **5 mcg/min**, increase **5 mcg/min every 3-5 min** (ceiling commonly quoted as 200 mcg/min)
Vasodilators only AFTER heart-rate control.
bank_lines: DocT: Nitroprusside releases 5 cyanide ions per molecule. Cyanide toxicity comes early (doses above ~2 µg/kg/min or low thiosulfate stores: lactic acidosis, high venous O2, confusion); thiocyanate builds up after 48–72 h or in renal failure (toxic >60 mg/L on a serum level). Stop the infusion; give hydroxocobalamin or sodium thiosulfate.

DocT GT: Prolonged nitroglycerin causes headache and reflex tachycardia, tachyphylaxis within 24 h, methaemoglobinaemia (its nitrite oxidises Hb) and inhibited platelet aggregation — but NOT cyanide toxicity, which belongs to nitroprusside.

explain.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Second-line doses and vasodilator toxicity
explain.intro: Step 5 ends with the vasodilators and the most-asked card in the deck: seven questions, six of them on what each drug does to the body with prolonged use. The key fact is the chemistry: nitroprusside carries cyanide, nitroglycerin carries nitrite.
why: a
**Diltiazem (non-DHP): 0.25 mg/kg over 2 min, then 5–10 mg/h, up to 15 mg/h.** It is the rate-controlling alternative when a beta-blocker is contraindicated.
b
**Nicardipine (DHP): 5 mg/h, increased by 2.5 mg/h every 5–15 min, max 15 mg/h.** A pure arterial dilator with no effect on the heart rate, so it follows the beta-blocker.
c

**Nitroprusside: 0.3 mcg/kg/min, max 10 mcg/kg/min (no more than 10 min at max); cyanide toxicity, unsuitable for prolonged use.** Each molecule releases five cyanide ions. Rhodanese uses thiosulfate to turn cyanide into thiocyanate, which the kidney excretes. Two toxicities follow. Cyanide comes early, at high doses (above about 2 mcg/kg/min) or when thiosulfate runs out: cells cannot use oxygen, so there is lactic acidosis, a high venous oxygen saturation, confusion and tachycardia. Thiocyanate builds up later, after 48–72 hours or in renal failure (toxic above about 60 mg/L on a serum level), causing confusion, psychosis and seizures. Stop the infusion and give hydroxocobalamin or sodium thiosulfate.
d

**Nitroglycerin: 5 mcg/min, increased by 5 mcg/min every 3–5 min (ceiling commonly quoted as 200 mcg/min).** Mostly a venodilator at low doses. Prolonged use causes headache, reflex tachycardia, tachyphylaxis within 24 hours, methaemoglobinaemia (its nitrite oxidises haemoglobin) and inhibition of platelet aggregation, but never cyanide toxicity.
mimic: Cyanide vs thiocyanate toxicity from nitroprusside
Cyanide: early, high dose, lactic acidosis and high venous saturation. Thiocyanate: late (48–72 h) or renal failure, neurotoxic, no lactic acidosis.
Hydroxocobalamin vs cyanocobalamin
Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to become cyanocobalamin, which is the harmless end product, not the antidote.
traps: GrandT1 keys “nitroglycerin” for confusion, tachycardia, acidosis and almond breath after a high-dose infusion (16% right)
The key is wrong: that is cyanide from nitroprusside, as the GT3 and AIM2 repeats and DocT’s own explanation say. Pick nitroprusside.
“Cyanide toxicity is a side effect of prolonged nitroglycerin” (41–43% right)
Nitroglycerin causes methaemoglobinaemia, headache, tachycardia and inhibited platelet aggregation; cyanide belongs to nitroprusside.
“Give thiocyanate” or “cyanocobalamin” for nitroprusside toxicity (39% right)
Thiocyanate is the toxic product, cyanocobalamin is what hydroxocobalamin becomes; the antidotes are sodium thiosulfate and hydroxocobalamin. Methylene blue treats methaemoglobinaemia.
“Urinary thiocyanate confirms it” (58% right)
Serum thiocyanate is the proper test, but among the four options it is still the best answer; an ABG shows acidosis but does not confirm the cause.
decode: 72 h of high-dose nitroprusside, altered sensorium, lactic acidosis — confirmatory test? [DocT QBank]
Thiocyanate level (58%).
Nitroprusside for 32 h in renal failure, confusion, acidosis — prevention/treatment? [DocT GT]
Sodium thiosulfate (39%).
Nitroglycerin drip for a day — least likely side effect? [DocT GT ×2]
Cyanide toxicity (41%, 43%).
High-dose infusion, confused, tachycardic, almond breath — drug? [DocT GT]
Nitroprusside (DocT keys nitroglycerin, 16%).
Most critical thing to monitor with prolonged nitroprusside [DocT GT]
Cyanide toxicity (95%).
Nitroglycerin infusion dose in hypertensive emergency [NEET 2024]
Start 5 mcg/min, titrate by 5 mcg/min every 3–5 min.
explain.punch: Nitroprusside carries five cyanides per molecule, so high doses or long infusions (especially in renal failure) cause lactic acidosis and confusion treated with thiosulfate or hydroxocobalamin; nitroglycerin carries nitrite, so it causes methaemoglobinaemia, never cyanide.

table.title: Nitroprusside vs nitroglycerin: the toxicity questions
head: Nitroprusside
Nitroglycerin
rows: Lactic acidosis, high venous O₂, confusion, almond breath
Headache, tachycardia, tachyphylaxis, cyanosis with normal PaO₂
Lactate, venous O₂; serum thiocyanate (cyanide: whole-blood level)

steps.q:
**For type A and type B dissection, give:**
a The preferred management
b Mortality with medical management
c Mortality with surgery
steps.a:
| **Type A** | **Type B**
**Preferred** | **SURGERY** | **MEDICAL**
**Medical mortality** | **~50%** | **~15%**
**Surgical mortality** | **15-20%** | **~30%**

explain.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Management and mortality by type
explain.intro: Step 6 starts with the decision between theatre and ICU. The numbers invert between types: surgery saves type A and harms uncomplicated type B. The real question is the same type A vignette as AD-06, testing what comes before the surgeon arrives.
why: a

**Preferred: SURGERY for type A, MEDICAL for type B.** Type A kills by tamponade, coronary occlusion and AR, which no drug fixes. Uncomplicated type B rarely ruptures early, and an operation on the descending aorta carries the risks of paraplegia, renal failure and a thoracotomy.
b

**Medical mortality: ~50% for type A, ~15% for type B.** ESC 2024 gives about 50% within 48 hours for untreated type A (1–2% per hour); IRAD 2000 gave 58% for medically treated type A and 10.7% for type B.
c

**Surgical mortality: 15–20% for type A, ~30% for type B.** ESC 2024 quotes 17–25% perioperative mortality for type A; IRAD 2000 gave 26% for type A and 31.4% for surgically treated type B. Surgery in type B is usually reserved for complicated cases, which partly explains the high figure; TEVAR has largely replaced it (AD-27).
mimic: Type A: drug first or surgery first?
Both: start anti-impulse therapy at once and go to surgery; drugs are a bridge, not the treatment.
traps: “Type A on CT — order a TEE” or “consult cardiology” before treatment (62% right)
The diagnosis is made; esmolol starts now and the surgeon is called.
“Surgery improves survival in all dissections”
Open surgery roughly doubles mortality in uncomplicated type B; medical therapy (then TEVAR if complicated or high risk) is preferred.
decode: Type A on CT, tachycardic, hypertensive — next best step? [DocT GT]
Start esmolol (62%), with urgent surgery.
Mortality of medically treated type A in the first 48 h [pattern]
About 50%, 1–2% per hour.
explain.punch: Type A goes to theatre because its killers are mechanical and mortality without surgery is about 50%; uncomplicated type B stays on drugs because surgery there roughly doubles mortality.

steps.q:
**List the five features that make an aortic**
**dissection "complicated".**
steps.a:
- **Rupture** or impending rupture
- **Intractable pain**
- **Malperfusion syndrome**
- **Cardiac tamponade**
- **Severe aortic valve insufficiency**

explain.intro: Step 3: ‘complicated’ is the label that moves a type B dissection from medical treatment to TEVAR (AD-27). Not asked directly.
why: a
**Rupture or impending rupture.** Blood outside the aorta (haemothorax, mediastinal or periaortic haematoma) or rapid expansion.
b
**Intractable pain.** Pain that persists or recurs despite full analgesia and anti-impulse therapy means the dissection is still extending.
c
**Malperfusion syndrome.** Organ or limb ischaemia from the false lumen (AD-05).
d
**Cardiac tamponade.** Rupture into the pericardium, a type A feature (AD-25).
e

**Severe aortic valve insufficiency.** Also type A. ESC 2024 also counts rapid aortic expansion, paraplegia, periaortic haematoma and uncontrolled hypertension; ‘high-risk’ uncomplicated type B (commonly cited features: aorta >40 mm, false lumen >20 mm, entry tear >10 mm) is a separate group that may get TEVAR in the subacute phase.
mimic: Complicated vs high-risk uncomplicated type B
Complicated (rupture, malperfusion, intractable pain) → TEVAR now (I, B); high-risk uncomplicated (large aorta or false lumen, large entry tear) → consider TEVAR at 14–90 days (IIa, B).
traps: “Hypertension alone makes a dissection complicated”
Only refractory hypertension despite full therapy is counted, and it signals ongoing extension.
decode: Type B with leg ischaemia or rising lactate — management? [pattern]
Complicated → TEVAR.
explain.punch: Rupture, intractable pain, malperfusion, tamponade or severe AR makes a dissection complicated, and in type B that means TEVAR rather than drugs alone.

steps.q:
**For type B dissection, give:**
a Initial management when uncomplicated
b Management when complicated
c When TEVAR is considered in uncomplicated
disease (2024 ESC)
d How TEVAR works
e The role of open surgery and its approach
steps.a:
- **MEDICAL** - anti-impulse therapy
- **TEVAR** (2024 ESC I/B with favourable anatomy); open
surgery the alternative
- Favourable anatomy → **TEVAR in the SUBACUTE phase**
(IIa/B)
- **Stent graft** seals the entry tear → false lumen **obliterates**
over time
- Only if unsuitable for endovascular repair (higher morbidity
and mortality) - **midline sternotomy** or **posterolateral
thoracotomy**, often on CPB

explain.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Type B: medical vs TEVAR
explain.intro: Step 6: type B splits by whether it is complicated. Not asked directly, but the notes contradict themselves, and the population resolves it.
why: a
**MEDICAL: anti-impulse therapy.** Beta-blocker to HR about 60, SBP below 120, analgesia, then oral beta-blockers after 24 hours if the gut works (ESC 2024).
b

**TEVAR (2024 ESC I/B with favourable anatomy); open surgery the alternative.** For complicated type B (rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain or hypertension, rapid expansion), TEVAR is first line (I, B).
c

**Favourable anatomy → TEVAR in the SUBACUTE phase (IIa/B).** ESC 2024: in selected uncomplicated patients with high-risk features (aorta >40 mm, false lumen >20 mm, entry tear >10 mm), TEVAR between 14 and 90 days (the ESC subacute phase, not IRAD’s 8–30 days, AD-08) improves aortic remodelling.
d
**Stent graft seals the entry tear → false lumen obliterates over time.** Covering the entry stops flow into the false lumen, which thromboses and shrinks while the true lumen expands.
e

**Only if unsuitable for endovascular repair (higher morbidity and mortality): midline sternotomy or posterolateral thoracotomy, often on CPB.** Open descending repair carries more paraplegia, renal failure and death.
mimic: Uncomplicated vs complicated type B
Uncomplicated: drugs (± TEVAR later if high risk); complicated: TEVAR now.
traps: “The primary treatment of type B is TEVAR”
Only when complicated or high-risk; uncomplicated type B is medical first.
decode: Type B with malperfusion or rupture [pattern]
TEVAR (I, B).
Uncomplicated type B with an aorta of 45 mm [pattern]
Medical, then consider TEVAR at 14–90 days (IIa, B).
explain.punch: Uncomplicated type B is treated with drugs, complicated type B with TEVAR at once, and high-risk uncomplicated type B with TEVAR in the subacute window; open surgery is the fallback.

steps.q:
**For surgical repair of type A dissection,**
**give:**
a Why surgery rather than endovascular repair
b What the operation does
c When the aortic valve is replaced (and the root size)
d The surgical access
steps.a:
- Proximity to the **aortic root** and involvement of the
**coronary origins** - makes endovascular repair challenging
- **Resect** the diseased segment → replace with a **synthetic
graft**
- Valve involved, **aortic insufficiency**, or dilated root **>55
mm** → simultaneous **aortic valve replacement**
- **Midline sternotomy**

explain.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Type A repair
explain.intro: Step 6: type A goes to open surgery because the problems are at the root, where stents cannot yet land safely. Not asked directly.
why: a

**Proximity to the aortic root and involvement of the coronary origins makes endovascular repair challenging.** A stent graft needs a healthy landing zone; the ascending aorta is short, close to the valve and the coronaries, and moves with each beat.
b

**Resect the diseased segment → replace with a synthetic graft.** At minimum, the entry tear in the ascending aorta is removed and the graft is sewn to the reconstructed root and to the arch; ESC 2024 recommends an open distal anastomosis (under circulatory arrest, AD-23) to improve survival and false-lumen thrombosis (I, B).
c

**Valve involved, aortic insufficiency, or dilated root >55 mm → simultaneous aortic valve replacement.** ESC 2024 and ACC/AHA 2022: when the leaflets are normal, resuspension of the valve is preferred over replacement; root replacement with a valved conduit is for root destruction, a root aneurysm or a genetic disorder such as Marfan (I, B).
d
**Midline sternotomy.** On cardiopulmonary bypass, often with axillary artery cannulation so that perfusion goes into the true lumen.
mimic: AR in type A: resuspend vs replace
Normal leaflets with commissural detachment → resuspend; destroyed root, aneurysm or connective-tissue disorder → root replacement.
traps: “AR in type A always means valve replacement”
Most AR in type A is from commissural detachment with normal leaflets and is fixed by resuspension.
decode: Why type A is not treated with a stent graft [pattern]
Root and coronary ostia: no safe landing zone.
explain.punch: Type A is repaired openly through a sternotomy, replacing the ascending aorta with a graft and resuspending the valve unless the root itself is destroyed or diseased.
